labels.name: repo-f3d8cfe4

labels.name: repo-f3d8cfe4

issue.body:
Currently, `r#crate`, `r#self`, `r#Self`, and `r#super` are prohibited regardless of circumstance. This is due to the fact that all four idents are allowed in paths and the fact that an identifier is raw is stripped away very early on in the compilation process.

A trivial attempt at bypassing that would have resulted in quite a bit of work, so I took a different approach: consider the four raw identifiers an identifier of their own. In other words, `r#self` is not the same as `self`, even though `r#foo` is the same as `foo`. This was surprisingly easy to implement…I only had to add four symbols and intercept them in the parser. Proc macros weren't much harder.

Other than tests specifically targeting the lack of support for these raw identifiers, no UI tests were altered.

As a language change, this will require FCP from T-lang. There's probably some other documentation that needs updating, in particular the reference, which is believed to explicitly document the current behavior. _Technically_ it involves changing the API of `proc_macro` in that more raw idents are supported, but that feels so trivial that T-libs doesn't need to be involved in my opinion.

cc @rust-lang/lang and @rust-lang/lang-advisors

[Initial discussion on Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/213817-t-lang/topic/.60crate.60.2C.20.60self.60.2C.20.60Self.60.2C.20and.20.60super.60.20cannot.20be.20raw.20idents.3F/near/639033584).

*[View all comments](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-comments/rust-lang/rust/pull/164731)*
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

Stabilize the following, including `const`:

```rust
// core::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;

// std::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;
```

The rename is happening in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/164730 (this is stacked on top).

There are three considerations for libs, which are the unresolved questions on the tracking issue:

1. Do we still want this even if we can eventually add `core::process::abort()` which calls to `libc::abort()` on platforms with an OS? I think yes: having effectively a single-instruction way to terminate is useful for performance reasons and as a fallback, e.g. running on an OS but without linking a `libc`.
2. What name do we want? Reception to `abort_immediate` seems lukewarm based on tracking issue discussion. I'm proposing we go with crash `crash` because it appears to be one of the more unobjectionable options there.
3. Should this live in `core::process` or somewhere else? There isn't really a process without an OS. But for consistency with `abort`, I think it is fine.

Lang is involved because this is stabilizing a new const intrinsic that can't _really_ be replicated with existing stable features, though `panic!()` is close.

Closes: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/154601 (tracking issue)

comment.body:
Nominating for T-libs discussion. I don't see any reason _not_ to add minutes and hours, particularly as leap seconds will effectively be abolished come May; those two should be noncontroversial. For days and weeks, the reason to not add them is that they vary in length for civil purposes, namely around DST/summer time changes in a number of locations.[^1] This is the same concern as the inherent associated consts and constructors, both of which are current implemented on nightly.

Personally, I (as maintainer of `time`) slightly favor the day and week API, defining it as a _nominal_ day/week, but I would not be disappointed if they were not added. Andrew (`jiff`) and Shane (`icu4x`) have both indicated opposition to inclusion in the standard library. If we decide to not add these, my recommendation is to remove the day/week constructors and consts from nightly, as asymmetry seems like the worst possible case.

[^1]: specifically nearly all of the US, eastern Canada (though I suspect this may be ending next year), border regions of Mexico, nearly all of Europe, The Bahamas, Cuba, Haiti, part of Chile, part of Australia, New Zealand, Egypt, Israel, Palestine, and Lebanon

Stabilize the following, including `const`:

```rust
// core::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;

// std::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;
```

The rename is happening in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/164730 (this is stacked on top).

There are three considerations for libs, which are the unresolved questions on the tracking issue:

1. Do we still want this even if we can eventually add `core::process::abort()` which calls to `libc::abort()` on platforms with an OS? I think yes: having effectively a single-instruction way to terminate is useful for performance reasons and as a fallback, e.g. running on an OS but without linking a `libc`.
2. What name do we want? Reception to `abort_immediate` seems lukewarm based on tracking issue discussion. I'm proposing we go with crash `crash` because it appears to be one of the more unobjectionable options there.
3. Should this live in `core::process` or somewhere else? There isn't really a process without an OS. But for consistency with `abort`, I think it is fine.

Lang is involved because this is stabilizing a new const intrinsic that can't _really_ be replicated with existing stable features, though `panic!()` is close.

Closes: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/154601 (tracking issue)

<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

<!--
Thank you for filing a regression report! 🐛 A regression is something that changed between versions of Rust but was not supposed to.

Please provide a short summary of the regression, along with any information you feel is relevant to replicate it.
-->

Zulip stream: https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/213817-t-lang/topic/Sealed.20generic.20traits.20are.20hard/with/637912566

----

Here is the [repo/code with the readme that contains all the details if you want to quickly reproduce the issue](https://github.com/Thomas-Mewily/rust_regression_when_compiling_that_emit_an_error_now).

I'm assuming it's a bug/regression, before stable Rust <= 1.97, the following code compile fine.
But after Rust >= 1.98, it produce a compile time error that make no sens.

### Code

I tried this code in a workspace containing 2 crates :

- crate `index_get` 
```rust
use std::ops::Index;

pub trait IndexGet<C> : Sized 
    where C: Index<Self>
{
    fn get(self, collection: &C) -> &C::Output  { collection.index(self) }
}
impl<I, C> IndexGet<C> for I where I: core::slice::SliceIndex<C>, C: Index<I> {}
```

- crate `custom_index` that depend on the first crate `index_get`
```rust
use std::ops::Index;
use index_get::IndexGet;

pub struct CustomIndex(usize);

impl<C> IndexGet<C> for CustomIndex where C: Index<CustomIndex> {}
```

### Version it worked on

This code compile fine on Rust 1.96 (and probably below?), 1.97:

```bash
rustup override set 1.98.0
cargo check
```

### Version with regression

However it don't work after Rust 1.98 and produce an compile time error :

```bash
rustup override set 1.98.0
cargo check
```

```rs
error[E0119]: conflicting implementations of trait `IndexGet<_>` for type `CustomIndex`
  --> custom_collection\src\lib.rs:15:1
   |
15 | impl<C> IndexGet<C> for CustomIndex where C: Index<CustomIndex>
   | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: conflicting implementation in crate `index_get`:
           - impl<I, C> IndexGet<C> for I
             where I: SliceIndex<C>, C: Index<I>;
   = note: downstream crates may implement trait `std::slice::SliceIndex<_>` for type `CustomIndex`
```

This error should not be possible to my knowledge, especially the `downstream crates may implement trait std::slice::SliceIndex<_> for type CustomIndex`.
Due to the [orphan rule](<https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/implementations.html#:~:text=either%20the%20trait%20or%20at%20least%20one%20of%20the%20types%20in%20the%20implementation%20is%20defined%20in%20the%20current%20crate>), it's impossible for a downstream crates to implement a foreign trait (`std::slice::SliceIndex<_>`) on a foreign type (`custom_collection::CustomIndex`).

```
rustc --version --verbose
rustc 1.98.0 (88d9e12ae 2026-08-18)
binary: rustc
commit-hash: 88d9e12ae178fab0fb5cc050a94da85685d449ea
commit-date: 2026-08-18
host: x86_64-pc-windows-gnu
release: 1.98.0
LLVM version: 22.1.8
```

<!--
Did the compiler crash? If so, please provide a backtrace.
-->

### When did that happen / Impact

This impacted some of my crates on crate.io that don't compile anymore :
(They are not used a lot so it's fine I guess)

https://crates.io/crates/hexga_generational (It define a similar trait `IndexGet` named `IndexExtension`)
https://crates.io/crates/hexga_core (It impl the trait for a custom index type named `UntypedGenIDOf`)

This is not new, it happen a few months ago (maybe >= 3 months ago ?).

At first I didn't pay too much attention because I was mainly working on nightly, and assumed it was a nightly bug, so I just rollback to an older version.

But I'm forced to admit that this regression is still present today on stable Rust.

-->

pinned_comment.body:
oooh wow i see now.

It doesn't matter that `Sealed` was hidden. Adding any supertrait makes this compile, as long as the supertrait is *not generic*: https://godbolt.org/z/31K163sW8

`impl<C> IndexGet<C> for CustomIndex where C: Index<CustomIndex> {}` can overlap with downstream crates doing `impl SliceIndex<LocalType> for CustomIndex {}`, which is why it errors without a supertrait.
But the supertrait (e.g. `Sealed`), which is not implemented for `CustomIndex`, makes this compile, as downstream crates would have to first do `impl Sealed for CustomIndex` to write the previous impl, which is a foreign trait for a foreign type and thus prevented by the orphan rule. Therefore `impl<C> IndexGet<C> for CustomIndex where C: Index<CustomIndex> {}` is allowed when there is a non-generic supertrait.

That is to say that the `SliceIndex` trait was not sealed correctly! 
This is super sneaky. I think we should document somewhere that for sealed generic traits, the sealing trait must be generic (and the generic parameters have to be used in the supertrait bound), otherwise it is a breaking change to unseal. 
We should also make sure all our other sealed generic traits are sealed correctly (if we have any left).

I guess we can add this to the list of "all orphan rule intuition goes out the window when generics are involved" ^^

```rust
use std::ops::Index;

    where C: Index<Self>
{
```

```rust

use index_get::IndexGet;

pub struct CustomIndex(usize);

```

```bash
cargo check
```

issue.body:
Inequalities like `x > T::MAX` for any integer type `T` in safety comments implicitly imply to be defined over the "mathematical" integers, whereas a regular reader may instead understand their meaning over `T` (and thus never become possibly satisfied). This discrepancy was raised on the stabilization PR for the `unchecked` methods on `NonZero`: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/164485#discussion_r4343552063.

I think removing the inequalities outright should be ok, because each safety comment refers to its `checked_*` counterpart. Similar methods dealing with overflow also do not give explicit bounds; but if you prefer, I can replace my changes with messages like "This results in undefined behavior when `x > T::MAX` over the mathematical integers (without wrapping around)".

This is a pre-1.0 attribute that accidentally got stabilized. It was only meant for compiler plugins which we no longer support, not for regular crates. issue.body:
<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
*[View all comments](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-comments/rust-lang/rust/pull/164458)*
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
- Intended to unblock https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/164384
- Also deals with https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/164348
- [Zulip thread](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/131828-t-compiler/topic/Hashing.20details.20from.20stage0.20stdlib.20leaking.20into.20stage1/with/632509711)
---
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

A subtle consequence of the stage0 redesign is that the compiler must take care to avoid relying on any stdlib-provided Hash impl when computing stable hashes, or at least any such impl that is actually liable to change.

This was noticed when trying to strengthen the provided Hash impl for Path, which triggered baffling CI failures because the stable hashes produced by the stage1 compiler (built against stage0 stdlib) were inconsistent with the ones that would have been produced by the stage2 compiler (built against in-tree stdlib).

This PR aims to unblock changes to `impl Hash for Path`, by making the compiler not rely on it for stable hashing. It does not attempt to solve the broader problem of the compiler relying on stdlib hash details.

<!-- homu-ignore:start -->
*[View all comments](https://triagebot.infra.rust-lang.org/gh-comments/rust-lang/rust/pull/164731)*
<!-- homu-ignore:end -->

Stabilize the following, including `const`:

```rust
// core::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;

// std::process
pub const fn crash() -> !;
```

The rename is happening in https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/164730 (this is stacked on top).

There are three considerations for libs, which are the unresolved questions on the tracking issue:

1. Do we still want this even if we can eventually add `core::process::abort()` which calls to `libc::abort()` on platforms with an OS? I think yes: having effectively a single-instruction way to terminate is useful for performance reasons and as a fallback, e.g. running on an OS but without linking a `libc`.
2. What name do we want? Reception to `abort_immediate` seems lukewarm based on tracking issue discussion. I'm proposing we go with crash `crash` because it appears to be one of the more unobjectionable options there.
3. Should this live in `core::process` or somewhere else? There isn't really a process without an OS. But for consistency with `abort`, I think it is fine.

Lang is involved because this is stabilizing a new const intrinsic that can't _really_ be replicated with existing stable features, though `panic!()` is close.

Closes: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/154601 (tracking issue)

comment.body: I actually _really_ like the name "crash". It's short and descriptive, particularly as opposed to "abort".
